sectionToMerge.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Radiation Therapy
sectionToMerge.intro: Radiation therapy is one of the most common cancer treatments worldwide. These answers explain what it is, how it works, and what patients and caregivers can expect.

items.a: Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment that uses high-energy rays or particles to damage cancer cells and stop them from growing or dividing. It is delivered in carefully measured doses aimed precisely at the tumour while sparing nearby healthy tissue as much as possible. Radiation may be used alone or alongside surgery, chemotherapy, or immunotherapy. The exact approach depends on cancer type, stage, location, and the treating oncology team's assessment.

items.q: How does radiation therapy work against cancer?
items.a: Radiation therapy works by damaging the DNA inside cancer cells so they can no longer multiply and eventually die. Cancer cells are often more sensitive to this damage than healthy cells and are less able to repair themselves. Treatment is usually divided into several small sessions, which gives normal tissue time to recover between doses. The goal, whether cure or symptom control, depends on the cancer type, stage, and overall treatment plan.

items.q: What are the main types of radiation therapy?
items.a: The two main types are external beam radiation therapy and internal radiation therapy (brachytherapy). External beam delivers radiation from a machine outside the body, while brachytherapy places a radioactive source inside or very close to the tumour. Advanced external techniques include IMRT, stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS/SBRT), and proton therapy. The most suitable type depends on cancer type, tumour location, stage, and specialist review by the radiation oncology team.

items.q: Why is radiation therapy used in cancer treatment?
items.a: Radiation therapy is used to destroy or shrink tumours, reduce the chance of cancer returning, or relieve symptoms such as pain and bleeding in advanced disease. It may be given to cure early cancers, to support surgery before or after an operation, or to control cancer that cannot be removed. Whether radiation is appropriate and its intended goal depend on the diagnosis, stage, and the treating oncology team's recommendation.

items.q: Who is eligible for radiation therapy?
items.a: Eligibility for radiation therapy depends on cancer type, stage, tumour location, previous treatments, and overall health, and is decided after specialist review. Many patients with solid tumours may be considered, while others may be better suited to surgery, chemotherapy, or a combination. Prior radiation to the same area can limit further treatment. A radiation oncologist reviews imaging, pathology, and medical history before confirming whether radiation therapy is a suitable option.

items.q: How is radiation therapy planned and given?
items.a: Radiation therapy usually begins with a planning session called simulation, where scans map the exact treatment area. The team then designs a precise plan and calculates the dose before treatment starts. External beam sessions are often given daily over several weeks, each lasting only minutes, and are painless during delivery. Planning and schedule vary by cancer type and technique, and are confirmed by the radiation oncology team based on individual needs.

Radiation therapy itself is not painful, and external beam sessions feel similar to having an X-ray taken. You lie still while the machine delivers treatment, and you do not see or feel the radiation. Some patients later develop side effects such as skin irritation or tiredness that can cause discomfort. Any pain related to treatment or the cancer should be discussed with the oncology team so it can be managed appropriately.

items.q: What are the common side effects of radiation therapy?
items.a: Common side effects of radiation therapy include tiredness, skin changes in the treated area, and symptoms specific to the region being treated, such as sore throat, nausea, or bladder irritation. Most side effects are temporary and improve after treatment ends, though some may appear later. Severity varies by dose, area treated, and individual health. The treating team monitors patients closely and offers supportive care to manage side effects.

items.q: How much does radiation therapy cost?
items.a: The cost of radiation therapy varies widely depending on the country, hospital, technique used, and number of sessions required. Advanced methods such as proton therapy or stereotactic radiosurgery generally cost more than standard external beam radiation. Final cost also depends on diagnosis, stage, additional tests, length of treatment, and any complications. Patients are advised to request a detailed written estimate from the treating hospital before starting treatment.

items.q: Is radiation therapy available in India?
items.a: Radiation therapy is widely available in India at many cancer hospitals, including advanced techniques such as IMRT, stereotactic radiosurgery, and brachytherapy. Some centres also offer proton therapy. India is often chosen by international patients because experienced facilities may be available at a lower cost than in many Western countries. Availability of a specific technique and suitability for an individual patient depend on the diagnosis and the treating oncology team's review.

items.q: Which countries offer advanced radiation therapy?
items.a: Advanced radiation therapy is offered in many countries, including India, the United States, Germany, the United Kingdom, Japan, China, and several others with dedicated cancer centres. Techniques such as proton therapy and stereotactic radiosurgery are available at selected specialised hospitals rather than everywhere. The best location depends on the type of treatment needed, cost, travel considerations, and specialist availability, and should be discussed with a qualified oncology team.

items.q: What is proton therapy and how is it different?
items.a: Proton therapy is an advanced form of external radiation that uses protons instead of X-rays to treat cancer. Its main advantage is that protons can deposit most of their energy directly in the tumour with less radiation to surrounding healthy tissue. This may be considered for tumours near sensitive organs or in children. Proton therapy is not suitable for every cancer, and eligibility is decided after specialist review of the individual case.

Stereotactic radiosurgery is a highly precise technique that delivers a strong dose of radiation to a small tumour in one or a few sessions. Despite the name, it involves no surgery or cutting. It is often used for brain tumours (SRS) or small tumours elsewhere in the body (SBRT). Suitability depends on tumour size, location, and number, and is determined by the radiation oncology team after detailed imaging and assessment.

items.q: Are there clinical trials for radiation therapy?
items.a: Yes, clinical trials study newer radiation techniques, dose schedules, and combinations with drugs such as immunotherapy. These trials aim to improve outcomes or reduce side effects, but they cannot guarantee benefit to any individual. Eligibility is decided only after medical record review and investigator assessment, and trials often have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria. Patients interested in trials should discuss suitable options with their treating oncology team.

items.q: What medical reports are needed to plan radiation therapy abroad?
items.a: Planning radiation therapy abroad usually requires recent imaging (such as CT, MRI, or PET scans), pathology or biopsy reports, and a summary of previous treatments. Details of prior radiation are especially important, as they affect what further treatment is possible. A clear medical history helps specialists give an accurate opinion and estimate. The treating hospital confirms the exact documents needed after an initial review of the patient's records.

items.q: How can international patients access radiation therapy in another country?
items.a: International patients can access radiation therapy abroad by first sharing their medical reports for a specialist opinion, then arranging hospital acceptance, cost estimates, and travel. Access depends on hospital acceptance, medical review, visa approval, and the patient's fitness to travel, none of which can be guaranteed in advance. Follow-up care planning is also important. A qualified oncology team makes the final treatment decision after reviewing the complete medical picture.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with radiation therapy?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centers, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, and overall health. This support is meant to guide patients through the process and does not replace the advice or care of doctors and hospitals.
